Reference: Allen and Arkolakis (2014)

Model Setting

The paper asks how much of the spatial disparity in economic activity is due to geographic location, that is, to how remote a place is from economic activity elsewhere, as opposed to the local characteristics (productivity and amenity) of the place itself. Earlier spatial models could answer this only on stylized geographies. The paper builds a general equilibrium framework that determines the distribution of population and wages on any surface with (nearly) any geography. The framework has two components that are distinct but compatible. The economic component combines the gravity structure of trade (an Armington model with perfect competition, as in Anderson 1979 and Anderson and van Wincoop 2003) with free labour mobility and with productivity and amenity spillovers that depend on local population. The geographic component microfounds bilateral trade costs as the accumulation of instantaneous trade costs along the least-cost route over the surface. Relative to Krugman (1991) the model has no homogeneous freely traded good, so nominal wages vary across space, and no monopolistic competition; it can also be read as the Roback (1982) model extended to costly trade.

The equilibrium is a system of integral equations. Without spillovers the system is linear and a unique equilibrium exists (Theorem 1). With spillovers and symmetric trade costs the system collapses to a single nonlinear integral equation of Hammerstein type, and the paper gives conditions on the spillover parameters for existence, uniqueness and stability (Theorem 2, Proposition 1); for particular spillover strengths the model is isomorphic to free-entry monopolistic competition, to the Helpman (1998) model with housing, and to models with land in production or heterogeneous locational preferences. Wages and population are log-linear in exogenous productivity, exogenous amenity and the price index, which is a sufficient statistic for geographic location. Applied to the continental United States, the paper estimates mode-specific trade costs from the road, rail, water and air networks with the Fast Marching Method and the 2007 Commodity Flow Survey, inverts the model to recover the topography of productivities and amenities of 3,109 counties in 2000 (Theorem 3), finds that geographic location accounts for at least 20 percent of the spatial variation in income, and estimates that removing the Interstate Highway System would lower welfare by 1.1 to 1.4 percent, far more than the cost of the system.

Environment

The world is a continuum of locations i∈Si\in Si∈S, where SSS is a closed bounded set of a finite-dimensional Euclidean space. Each location produces a unique differentiated variety (the Armington assumption). Trade costs are of the iceberg form: T(i,j)≥1T(i,j)\geq1T(i,j)≥1 units must be shipped from iii for one unit to arrive in jjj, with T(i,i)=1T(i,i)=1T(i,i)=1. A measure Lˉ\bar{L}Lˉ of workers is freely mobile across locations. Workers have identical constant elasticity of substitution preferences over varieties, and welfare in location iii is:

W(i)=(∫s∈Sq(s,i)σ−1σds)σσ−1u(i)(1)W(i)=\left(\int_{s\in S}q(s,i)^{\frac{\sigma-1}{\sigma}}ds\right)^{\frac{\sigma}{\sigma-1}}u(i) \tag{1}W(i)=(∫s∈S​q(s,i)σσ−1​ds)σ−1σ​u(i)(1)

where q(s,i)q(s,i)q(s,i) is the per capita quantity of the variety produced in sss and consumed in iii, σ∈(1,∞)\sigma\in(1,\infty)σ∈(1,∞) is the elasticity of substitution and u(i)u(i)u(i) is the local amenity. Labour is the only factor. Each worker supplies one unit of labour inelastically where she lives and produces A(i)A(i)A(i) units of the local variety, and production is perfectly competitive. The functions L(i)L(i)L(i) and w(i)w(i)w(i) are the density of workers and the wage. Productivity and amenity may depend on local population:

A(i)=Aˉ(i)L(i)α,u(i)=uˉ(i)L(i)β(2)A(i)=\bar{A}(i)L(i)^{\alpha},\qquad u(i)=\bar{u}(i)L(i)^{\beta} \tag{2}A(i)=Aˉ(i)L(i)α,u(i)=uˉ(i)L(i)β(2)

where Aˉ(i)\bar{A}(i)Aˉ(i) and uˉ(i)\bar{u}(i)uˉ(i) are the exogenous components, α\alphaα is the strength of the productivity spillover and β\betaβ the strength of the amenity spillover. Both are real numbers, and the paper focuses on the empirically relevant case α≥0\alpha\geq0α≥0 and β≤0\beta\leq0β≤0. The spillovers are local: they do not affect nearby locations. A(i)A(i)A(i) and u(i)u(i)u(i) are called composite (overall) productivity and amenity.

The geography of SSS is the set of functions Aˉ\bar{A}Aˉ, uˉ\bar{u}uˉ and TTT; the first two are the local characteristics and TTT is the geographic location. A geography is regular if the three functions are continuous and bounded above and below by strictly positive numbers. The distribution of economic activity is the pair of functions www and LLL, with the normalization ∫Sw(s)ds=1\int_Sw(s)ds=1∫S​w(s)ds=1. The topography of the spatial economy is the geography together with the distribution of economic activity.

Isomorphisms

The spillovers are assumed and not microfounded, and the paper shows (in its Online Appendix A.2, summarized in the main text) that particular values of α\alphaα and β\betaβ make the model isomorphic to other spatial models in trade flows, wages, population and welfare, though not necessarily in other dimensions.

  • Monopolistic competition with free entry: if α=1σ−1\alpha=\frac{1}{\sigma-1}α=σ−11​ the model is isomorphic to a model with differentiated varieties and free entry in which the number of varieties produced in a location is proportional to its population, as in Krugman (1980, 1991). The productivity spillover is then the agglomeration externality from more entry in larger markets: with N(i)N(i)N(i) varieties proportional to L(i)L(i)L(i), the price index of goods from iii falls with N(i)11−σN(i)^{\frac{1}{1-\sigma}}N(i)1−σ1​, exactly as if productivity were proportional to L(i)1σ−1L(i)^{\frac{1}{\sigma-1}}L(i)σ−11​.

  • Non-tradable housing: if α=1σ−1\alpha=\frac{1}{\sigma-1}α=σ−11​ and β=−1−δδ\beta=-\frac{1-\delta}{\delta}β=−δ1−δ​ the model is isomorphic to Helpman (1998) and Redding (2012), where 1−δ1-\delta1−δ is the budget share spent on an immobile factor such as land or housing. The negative β\betaβ captures the inelastic supply of housing: more residents raise the housing price, which lowers utility like a congestion externality.

  • Land in production: if α=δ−1\alpha=\delta-1α=δ−1, where δ\deltaδ is here the labour share in a Cobb-Douglas production function with land, the (negative) productivity spillover captures diminishing returns to labour.

  • Heterogeneous locational preferences: if workers draw idiosyncratic preferences for locations from an extreme value distribution, the amenity spillover measures how much workers differ in these preferences. With a Frechet shape parameter this corresponds to β\betaβ equal to minus the inverse of that parameter, since the marginal resident of a larger location has a lower idiosyncratic taste for it; the main text states the isomorphism without this formula.

  • Costless trade: when trade is costless the equilibrium conditions coincide with versions of the Roback (1982) model.

Entry, housing and preference heterogeneity can be combined, so the two numbers α\alphaα and β\betaβ summarize the net agglomeration and dispersion forces of a wide class of models. The trade side is an Armington model with trade elasticity σ−1\sigma-1σ−1; the choice σ=9\sigma=9σ=9 in the empirical part gives a trade elasticity of 8, in line with Eaton and Kortum (2002).

Equilibrium without Spillovers

When α=β=0\alpha=\beta=0α=β=0 and welfare is equalized at WWW, the two equations are linear in the unknown functions L(i)w(i)σL(i)w(i)^{\sigma}L(i)w(i)σ and w(i)1−σw(i)^{1-\sigma}w(i)1−σ. For instance, the second equation can be rewritten (in shorthand that is not in the paper) as:

Wσ−1w(i)1−σ=∫SK(s,i)w(s)1−σds,K(s,i)≡T(s,i)1−σAˉ(s)σ−1uˉ(i)σ−1(10)W^{\sigma-1}w(i)^{1-\sigma}=\int_SK(s,i)w(s)^{1-\sigma}ds,\qquad K(s,i)\equiv T(s,i)^{1-\sigma}\bar{A}(s)^{\sigma-1}\bar{u}(i)^{\sigma-1} \tag{10}Wσ−1w(i)1−σ=∫S​K(s,i)w(s)1−σds,K(s,i)≡T(s,i)1−σAˉ(s)σ−1uˉ(i)σ−1(10)

so w(i)1−σw(i)^{1-\sigma}w(i)1−σ is an eigenfunction of a linear integral operator with a strictly positive continuous kernel and Wσ−1W^{\sigma-1}Wσ−1 is the associated eigenvalue. The first equation has L(i)w(i)σL(i)w(i)^{\sigma}L(i)w(i)σ as eigenfunction, the same eigenvalue Wσ−1W^{\sigma-1}Wσ−1, and a kernel that is the transpose of KKK.

Theorem 1. For a regular geography with exogenous productivities and amenities, (i) there exists a unique spatial equilibrium and it is regular; (ii) it can be computed as the uniform limit of a simple iterative procedure.

The proof is in Online Appendix A.1.1 of the paper. Its logic, as described in the text, is that the two equations are a linear system for which extensions of standard results of linear algebra guarantee a unique positive solution: the continuum analogue of the Perron-Frobenius theorem (Jentzsch's theorem, which the appendix invokes in its generalized form for linear eigenequations) says that a positive kernel has a unique strictly positive eigenfunction, up to scale, and that it belongs to the largest eigenvalue. Positivity delivers regularity (L(i)>0L(i)>0L(i)>0 everywhere), the scale of www is fixed by the wage normalization and the scale of LLL by aggregate labour market clearing. Because the positive eigenfunction belongs to the dominant eigenvalue, repeatedly applying the operator to any positive initial guess converges to it, so no good starting guess is needed. Welfare is an eigenvalue: the equilibrium welfare level is pinned down by the largest eigenvalue of the kernel built from trade costs, productivities and amenities, so better geography in any of the three senses raises WWW.

Second, as long as γ1>0\gamma_1>0γ1​>0, population is higher where exogenous productivity and amenity are high and where the price index is low. Wages may rise or fall with exogenous productivity depending on the sign of β\betaβ, and with exogenous amenity and the price index depending on the signs of 1−α(σ−1)1-\alpha(\sigma-1)1−α(σ−1) and 1+(σ−1)(β−α)1+(\sigma-1)(\beta-\alpha)1+(σ−1)(β−α). Third, conditional on the price index, spillovers only change the elasticity of economic activity with respect to geography: if γ1>0\gamma_1>0γ1​>0, larger α\alphaα or β\betaβ lowers γ1\gamma_1γ1​ and makes population more sensitive to geographic differences. The price index is itself endogenous, so unless trade is free the spillovers also act through general equilibrium effects on it.

Efficiency

The appendix compares the competitive equilibrium with a planner who chooses trade flows and population to maximize total utility:

Proposition 2 of the appendix states that the competitive distribution of population solves the planner's problem if and only if α+β=0\alpha+\beta=0α+β=0. Workers ignore the productivity and amenity externalities they impose; the two externalities offset exactly when α+β=0\alpha+\beta=0α+β=0, which is also the boundary of the uniqueness region.

Geographic Trade Costs

The geographic component gives a microfoundation for TTT. Let SSS be a compact manifold (a line, a circle or a plane in the applications) and let τ(i)\tau(i)τ(i) be a continuous function giving the instantaneous trade cost of crossing point iii. The cost of the least-cost path between iii and jjj is:

t(i,j)=inf⁡g∈Γ(i,j)∫01τ(g(t))∥dg(t)dt∥dt(24)t(i,j)=\inf_{g\in\Gamma(i,j)}\int_0^1\tau\left(g(t)\right)\left\|\frac{dg(t)}{dt}\right\|dt \tag{24}t(i,j)=g∈Γ(i,j)inf​∫01​τ(g(t))​dtdg(t)​​dt(24)

where g:[0,1]→Sg:[0,1]\rightarrow Sg:[0,1]→S is a path, Γ(i,j)\Gamma(i,j)Γ(i,j) is the set of continuous and once differentiable paths with g(0)=ig(0)=ig(0)=i and g(1)=jg(1)=jg(1)=j, and the norm is Euclidean. Bilateral trade costs are geographic if T(i,j)=f(t(i,j))T(i,j)=f\left(t(i,j)\right)T(i,j)=f(t(i,j)) for a monotonically increasing function fff with f(0)=1f(0)=1f(0)=1. Then the function τ\tauτ on SSS determines the function TTT on S×SS\times SS×S, which reduces the dimensionality of the problem by its square root. Roads and railways are represented by low values of τ\tauτ, borders by walls of high τ\tauτ (which can also line a road so that it is accessible only at entrance ramps), and natural geography by ruggedness or water. Geographic trade costs are symmetric, because crossing a point costs the same in both directions, and nearby locations face similar costs to all destinations, lim⁡s→iT(s,j)=T(i,j)\lim_{s\rightarrow i}T(s,j)=T(i,j)lims→i​T(s,j)=T(i,j). They abstract from non-geographic costs such as tariffs or information frictions, which are added back in the estimation.

The solution of the path problem is characterized by the eikonal equation:

∥∇t(i,j)∥=τ(j)(25)\left\|\nabla t(i,j)\right\|=\tau(j) \tag{25}∥∇t(i,j)∥=τ(j)(25)

where the gradient is taken with respect to the destination jjj. Consider the iso-cost contour {j∣t(i,j)=C}\left\{j|t(i,j)=C\right\}{j∣t(i,j)=C}. As CCC rises the contour expands outward, orthogonally to itself, at a speed inversely proportional to the instantaneous trade cost, like a wave front propagating from the origin. This gives an algorithm, the Fast Marching Method (Sethian 1996, 1999): from each point jjj of a contour draw a vector of length ετ(j)\frac{\varepsilon}{\tau(j)}τ(j)ε​ orthogonal to the contour; connecting the ends of these vectors gives the contour at cost C+εC+\varepsilonC+ε; starting from an arbitrarily small contour around iii and iterating gives the cost from iii to every destination. Because τ\tauτ is positive, costs always increase as one marches outward, so each contour is built from the previous one only. The run time is O(nlog⁡n)O(n\log n)O(nlogn) in the number of pixels nnn that approximate τ\tauτ: less than a second per origin even at high resolution, and a couple of hours for all origins. The method generalizes the Dijkstra algorithm to continuous space and avoids its digitization bias, the upward bias in distances that arises because a grid restricts the directions of travel. It also extends to instantaneous costs that depend on the direction of travel (elevation, one-way roads), since the direction of each vector depends only on the slope of the contour and its length only on the cost; bilateral costs are then no longer symmetric and Theorem 2 does not apply.

The paper uses the exponential form:

T(i,j)=et(i,j)(26)T(i,j)=e^{t(i,j)} \tag{26}T(i,j)=et(i,j)(26)

which is the limit of the product of many incremental iceberg costs as the distance between increments goes to zero, so it microfounds the iceberg form of bilateral costs. More generally, the appendix proves that for monotonically increasing fff with f(0)=1f(0)=1f(0)=1, the triangle inequality T(i,k)≤T(i,j)T(j,k)T(i,k)\leq T(i,j)T(j,k)T(i,k)≤T(i,j)T(j,k) holds for all locations if and only if fff is log subadditive:

ln⁡f(x+y)≤ln⁡f(x)+ln⁡f(y)(27)\ln f(x+y)\leq\ln f(x)+\ln f(y) \tag{27}lnf(x+y)≤lnf(x)+lnf(y)(27)

for all xxx and yyy between zero and half the maximum distance in SSS. Sufficiency uses the fact that the least-cost distance itself satisfies t(i,k)≤t(i,j)+t(j,k)t(i,k)\leq t(i,j)+t(j,k)t(i,k)≤t(i,j)+t(j,k) together with the monotonicity of fff; necessity uses the fact that any pair xxx and yyy can be realized by a point jjj on the least-cost route between two locations.

The Line

Combining the two components gives closed-form examples. Let SSS be the interval [−π,π][-\pi,\pi][−π,π], with no spillovers and Aˉ(i)=uˉ(i)=1\bar{A}(i)=\bar{u}(i)=1Aˉ(i)=uˉ(i)=1. The instantaneous trade cost is a constant τ\tauτ except for a border of cost bbb in the middle of the line:

This TTT is discontinuous, so the theorems do not apply, but an explicit solution exists. Differentiating the log population equation gives:

At the far left, moving right reduces the distance to all other locations and so lowers the log price index at rate τ\tauτ. Differentiating the Hammerstein equation twice (the exponential kernel reproduces itself under differentiation) gives a second-order differential equation:

∂2∂i2L(i)σ~=k1L(i)σ~ for i∈(−π,0)∪(0,π),k1≡(1−σ)2τ2+2(1−σ)τW1−σ(31)\frac{\partial^2}{\partial i^2}L(i)^{\tilde{\sigma}}=k_1L(i)^{\tilde{\sigma}}\ \text{for}\ i\in(-\pi,0)\cup(0,\pi),\qquad k_1\equiv(1-\sigma)^2\tau^2+2(1-\sigma)\tau W^{1-\sigma} \tag{31}∂i2∂2​L(i)σ~=k1​L(i)σ~ for i∈(−π,0)∪(0,π),k1​≡(1−σ)2τ2+2(1−σ)τW1−σ(31)

The boundary conditions determine k1k_1k1​ (and hence welfare) and the ratio of k2k_2k2​ to k3k_3k3​, and aggregate labour market clearing determines their levels. With no border the solution is a single cosine and k3=0k_3=0k3​=0; with an infinite border it is two cosines, one centred in each half.

The figures of the paper illustrate the comparative statics. Without a border (Figure III, σ=4\sigma=4σ=4), population is uniform when τ=0\tau=0τ=0 and concentrates more and more in the centre, where the price index is lowest, as τ\tauτ rises from 1 to 3; wages are lower in the centre to compensate for the lower price index. A border (Figure IV, border cost 0.1 and 0.5) moves population toward the middle of each half, and in the limit of an infinite border the two halves behave as isolated lines. If productivity rises to the right, Aˉ(i)=eAσ−1i\bar{A}(i)=e^{\frac{A}{\sigma-1}i}Aˉ(i)=eσ−1A​i, the differential equation becomes (the paper prints AiAiAi for the first term, which is the term in the level of ln⁡L(i)\ln L(i)lnL(i)):

∂ln⁡L(i)∂i=A+(1−2σ)∂ln⁡P(i)∂i(33)\frac{\partial\ln L(i)}{\partial i}=A+(1-2\sigma)\frac{\partial\ln P(i)}{\partial i} \tag{33}∂i∂lnL(i)​=A+(1−2σ)∂i∂lnP(i)​(33)

and population shifts to the right when A>0A>0A>0 (Figure V); the solution can be written with Bessel functions of the first and second kind. Raising α\alphaα with homogeneous productivity (Figure VI, α\alphaα from 0 to 0.4 with β=0\beta=0β=0) concentrates population in the centre as long as γ1>0\gamma_1>0γ1​>0. Once γ1<0\gamma_1<0γ1​<0 the regular equilibrium is completely different, with most people at the two edges, and it is not point-wise locally stable because a few workers could move to the centre and be better off. If travelling to the right costs more than travelling to the left, population shifts to the left, where the price index is lowest (Figure VII).

The Circle and the Fourier Approximation

The circle illustrates multiplicity. When α+β=0\alpha+\beta=0α+β=0 the unique equilibrium has uniform population. When α+β>0\alpha+\beta>0α+β>0 (the example uses α=0.01\alpha=0.01α=0.01 and β=0\beta=0β=0) the uniform distribution remains an equilibrium but there is also a continuum of equilibria, each with population concentrated around a different point. The point α+β=0\alpha+\beta=0α+β=0 is therefore a bifurcation point, and with α+β>0\alpha+\beta>0α+β>0 higher trade costs can act as an additional agglomeration force. If γ1\gamma_1γ1​ turns negative the only known regular equilibrium is again the symmetric one, and it is unstable.

The appendix characterizes the circle with two symmetric borders and no spillovers by a perturbation method that follows Fabinger (2011). The equilibrium is written as the eigenequation:

λy(x)=∫T(x,x′)y(x′)dx′(34)\lambda y(x)=\int T(x,x')y(x')dx' \tag{34}λy(x)=∫T(x,x′)y(x′)dx′(34)

where in this section of the appendix TTT denotes the kernel and not the trade cost. On the circle with domain (−π,π)(-\pi,\pi)(−π,π) the kernel is e(1−σ)τd(θ,θ′)e^{(1-\sigma)\tau d(\theta,\theta')}e(1−σ)τd(θ,θ′), where d(θ,θ′)d(\theta,\theta')d(θ,θ′) is the shorter arc between θ\thetaθ and θ′\theta'θ′. Country A occupies (−π/2,π/2)(-\pi/2,\pi/2)(−π/2,π/2) and country B the rest. The border perturbs the kernel to T(x,x′)+κt(x,x′)T(x,x')+\kappa t(x,x')T(x,x′)+κt(x,x′), where κ\kappaκ is small and ttt equals minus the kernel for pairs in different countries and zero otherwise. Because GGG depends only on θ−θ′\theta-\theta'θ−θ′, the convolution theorem turns the operator series into a geometric series for each Fourier coefficient of y1y_1y1​. The coefficients vanish for odd nnn and for n=0n=0n=0, and summing the series for even nnn with standard identities gives the closed form:

y1(x)=(σ−1)τ2π(π212−x2) for −π2≤x≤π2(38)y_1(x)=\frac{(\sigma-1)\tau}{2\pi}\left(\frac{\pi^2}{12}-x^2\right)\ \text{for}\ -\frac{\pi}{2}\leq x\leq\frac{\pi}{2} \tag{38}y1​(x)=2π(σ−1)τ​(12π2​−x2) for −2π​≤x≤2π​(38)

The result is an approximation because the eigenvalue itself changes with the parameters.

Multiple Sectors

In the line and circle examples lower trade costs disperse activity, as in Helpman (1998), whereas in Krugman (1991) and Fujita, Krugman and Venables (1999) lower trade costs produce a core-periphery pattern. The paper attributes the difference to the second sector with zero trade costs in those models, and the appendix adds a second sector to show it. With sectors l=1,2l=1,2l=1,2, Cobb-Douglas expenditure shares that the appendix writes γ1\gamma_1γ1​ and γ2\gamma_2γ2​ (summing to one, and unrelated to the composite parameters above), and no spillovers, the sectoral price index and welfare are:

Pl(i)1−σ=∫STl(s,i)1−σAl(s)σ−1w(s)1−σds,W(i)=w(i)(P1(i))γ1(P2(i))γ2u(i)(39)P_l(i)^{1-\sigma}=\int_ST_l(s,i)^{1-\sigma}A_l(s)^{\sigma-1}w(s)^{1-\sigma}ds,\qquad W(i)=\frac{w(i)}{\left(P_1(i)\right)^{\gamma_1}\left(P_2(i)\right)^{\gamma_2}}u(i) \tag{39}Pl​(i)1−σ=∫S​Tl​(s,i)1−σAl​(s)σ−1w(s)1−σds,W(i)=(P1​(i))γ1​(P2​(i))γ2​w(i)​u(i)(39)

and market clearing is, as printed:

Welfare equalization involves wages only, and given wages market clearing is linear in LLL with a positive kernel, so it has a unique solution. Existence and uniqueness therefore reduce to welfare equalization, which with f(i)=w(i)1−σf(i)=w(i)^{1-\sigma}f(i)=w(i)1−σ and λ=Wˉσ−1\lambda=\bar{W}^{\sigma-1}λ=Wˉσ−1 reads:

λf(i)=(K1f(i))γ1(K2f(i))γ2,Klf(i)=∫STl(s,i)1−σu(i)σ−1Al(s)σ−1f(s)ds(41)\lambda f(i)=\left(K_1f(i)\right)^{\gamma_1}\left(K_2f(i)\right)^{\gamma_2},\qquad K_lf(i)=\int_ST_l(s,i)^{1-\sigma}u(i)^{\sigma-1}A_l(s)^{\sigma-1}f(s)ds \tag{41}λf(i)=(K1​f(i))γ1​(K2​f(i))γ2​,Kl​f(i)=∫S​Tl​(s,i)1−σu(i)σ−1Al​(s)σ−1f(s)ds(41)

Proposition 3 of the appendix states that a unique wage function and a unique welfare level solve it. Existence follows from applying the Schauder fixed point theorem to the normalized operator on the closed convex set of non-negative, bounded, continuous functions that integrate to one; the operator maps this set into itself, is continuous, and is compact by the Arzela-Ascoli theorem (its image is bounded and equicontinuous). Uniqueness of the eigenvalue follows from comparing the growth rates of iterates started from two positive eigenfunctions, and uniqueness of the eigenfunction from a contradiction argument at a point where two candidate solutions touch. On the line [−1,1][-1,1][−1,1] with Tj(i,s)=exp⁡(τj∣i−s∣)T_j(i,s)=\exp\left(\tau_j|i-s|\right)Tj​(i,s)=exp(τj​∣i−s∣), σ=4\sigma=4σ=4 and equal shares, raising trade costs in either sector concentrates population when both sectors have positive trade costs, but when the second sector is freely traded raising the cost in the first sector reduces concentration: more workers move into the freely traded sector, whose price index is equal across space, and this dispersion force dominates.

Data and Trade Cost Estimation

The empirical part recovers the geography of the continental United States in two steps, with σ=9\sigma=9σ=9 throughout. Three kinds of data are used. The transport networks cover 650,000 km of interstates, other highways and arterial roads, about 225,000 km of railways and about 300,000 km of navigable waterways, projected onto a 1,032 by 760 pixel image of the country. Bilateral trade flows by mode come from the 2007 Commodity Flow Survey (CFS), with each CFS area treated as a location. Wages and population of 3,109 counties come from the 2000 Census. Counties are taken as locations to balance the accuracy of the discrete approximation against computation and against the assumptions of no commuting and no spatial spillovers, which become less plausible for small units.

Mode-specific distances. For each mode mmm (road, rail, water, air) an instantaneous cost function τm\tau_mτm​ assigns a low value on the network and a high value off it (details in Online Appendix B.3), and the Fast Marching Method gives a normalized distance dm(i,j)d_m(i,j)dm​(i,j) between every pair, scaled so that crossing the width of the country along a straight route on the network costs one. In reduced-form regressions with origin and destination fixed effects, the log value of road shipments falls strongly with log road distance (elasticity about 1.37 in absolute value, 9,177 observations), also conditional on straight-line distance, and rises with water distance, which suggests substitution across modes.

Discrete choice over modes. For each pair a mass of identical traders choose the mode that minimizes the iceberg cost of shipping one unit, which for trader ttt and mode mmm is exp⁡(τmdm(i,j)+fm+νtm)\exp\left(\tau_md_m(i,j)+f_m+\nu_{tm}\right)exp(τm​dm​(i,j)+fm​+νtm​): τm\tau_mτm​ is the mode-specific variable cost, fmf_mfm​ the mode-specific cost that is fixed with respect to distance and νtm\nu_{tm}νtm​ an idiosyncratic cost, independent across traders and modes with a Gumbel distribution of shape θ\thetaθ:

Pr⁡{ν≤x}=e−e−θx(42)\Pr\left\{\nu\leq x\right\}=e^{-e^{-\theta x}} \tag{42}Pr{ν≤x}=e−e−θx(42)

so that, in the paper's words, eνe^{\nu}eν is Frechet with shape θ\thetaθ (the closed forms below hold exactly when this is read as the distribution of −ν-\nu−ν, so that eνe^{\nu}eν is Weibull). The fraction of trade from iii to jjj shipped by mode mmm is then:

πm(i,j)=exp⁡(−amdm(i,j)−bm)∑kexp⁡(−akdk(i,j)−bk)(43)\pi_m(i,j)=\frac{\exp\left(-a_md_m(i,j)-b_m\right)}{\sum_k\exp\left(-a_kd_k(i,j)-b_k\right)} \tag{43}πm​(i,j)=∑k​exp(−ak​dk​(i,j)−bk​)exp(−am​dm​(i,j)−bm​)​(43)

where am≡θτma_m\equiv\theta\tau_mam​≡θτm​ and bm≡θfmb_m\equiv\theta f_mbm​≡θfm​. The parameters ama_mam​ and bmb_mbm​ are estimated by nonlinear least squares on observed mode shares, with the fixed cost of road normalized to zero. This framework is separate from the geography model and is used only to measure trade costs. Its advantage is identification from mode shares within an origin-destination pair, which controls for the level of bilateral trade in the same way as a pair fixed effect and so mitigates the concern that networks are built where trade is large; the concern that networks are placed where a particular mode is in demand remains. The average geographic trade cost implied by the discrete choice is:

Gravity regression. Mode shares identify costs only up to the scale θ\thetaθ. Total trade costs combine TgT_gTg​ with non-geographic costs that depend on a vector of bilateral observables C(i,j)\mathbf{C}(i,j)C(i,j). Taking logs of the gravity equation gives:

where δi\delta_iδi​ and δj\delta_jδj​ are origin and destination fixed effects, and β\betaβ here is the vector of coefficients on the observables, not the amenity spillover. Given σ\sigmaσ, the coefficient on the first term identifies θ\thetaθ, and hence τm\tau_mτm​ and fmf_mfm​. A different trade elasticity would only rescale the estimates, since trade flows are matched equally well by a high elasticity with low costs or the reverse. Standard errors come from 1,000 bootstrap repetitions of the whole procedure.

Estimates (all CFS areas, 9,601 pairs with positive flows). The variable costs are 0.5636 for road, 0.1434 for rail, 0.0779 for water and 0.0026 for air; the fixed costs are 0 for road (normalized), 0.4219 for rail, 0.5407 for water and 0.5734 for air; the shape parameter is 14.225 with standard error 0.3375. The mode-specific bilateral cost is the exponential of variable cost times distance plus fixed cost, so road is the cheapest mode at every distance, but the other modes become relatively cheaper as distance grows, matching the declining road share. The magnitudes are comparable to the 55 percent domestic distribution cost of Anderson and van Wincoop (2004). The coefficients on non-geographic observables are −0.0888-0.0888−0.0888 for similar ethnicity, 0.063 for similar language, −0.0191-0.0191−0.0191 for similar migrants (not significant) and −0.2984-0.2984−0.2984 for same state: costs are about 30 percentage points lower within a state. The sample of metropolitan areas only (3,266 pairs) gives similar numbers, with shape parameter 17.6509. Predicted flows explain 65 percent of the variation in observed flows (overall R-squared 0.6456, within 0.4487), and the residuals are uncorrelated with straight-line distance, which supports the exponential form.

Identification of Productivities and Amenities

Theorem 3. For any continuous functions www and LLL and any continuous symmetric function TTT, all bounded above and below by strictly positive numbers, there exist unique (to scale) positive and continuous functions AAA and uuu such that www and LLL are the regular spatial equilibrium for the geography defined by TTT, Aˉ=AL−α\bar{A}=AL^{-\alpha}Aˉ=AL−α and uˉ=uL−β\bar{u}=uL^{-\beta}uˉ=uL−β (proof in Online Appendix A.1.5).

Rearranging the two equilibrium equations shows the structure of the inversion (this rearrangement is not displayed in the paper):

A(i)1−σ=W1−σL(i)w(i)σ∫ST(i,s)1−σu(s)σ−1L(s)w(s)σdsu(i)1−σ=W1−σw(i)1−σ∫ST(s,i)1−σA(s)σ−1w(s)1−σds(46)\begin{aligned} A(i)^{1-\sigma}&=\frac{W^{1-\sigma}}{L(i)w(i)^{\sigma}}\int_ST(i,s)^{1-\sigma}u(s)^{\sigma-1}L(s)w(s)^{\sigma}ds\\ u(i)^{1-\sigma}&=\frac{W^{1-\sigma}}{w(i)^{1-\sigma}}\int_ST(s,i)^{1-\sigma}A(s)^{\sigma-1}w(s)^{1-\sigma}ds \end{aligned} \tag{46}A(i)1−σu(i)1−σ​=L(i)w(i)σW1−σ​∫S​T(i,s)1−σu(s)σ−1L(s)w(s)σds=w(i)1−σW1−σ​∫S​T(s,i)1−σA(s)σ−1w(s)1−σds​(46)

Given data on www, LLL and TTT, productivities are determined by amenities elsewhere and amenities by productivities elsewhere, and the theorem says that this system has exactly one positive solution up to scale. The theorem does not use the functional form of the spillovers: it recovers the composite AAA and uuu, and any known relation between spillovers and population (including spillovers across space) can then be inverted to obtain the exogenous components. The converse is that α\alphaα and β\betaβ cannot be identified from a cross-section of wages and population: for any α\alphaα and β\betaβ there are functions Aˉ\bar{A}Aˉ and uˉ\bar{u}uˉ that rationalize the data, the same point that Ellison and Glaeser (1997) make about natural advantage and spillovers. The theorem also justifies the sequential strategy of estimating trade costs first.

The intuition uses two locations iii and jjj with the same geographic location, T(i,s)=T(j,s)T(i,s)=T(j,s)T(i,s)=T(j,s) for all sss. They face the same price index, so the ratio of nominal wages equals the ratio of real wages, and since welfare is equalized relative amenities are the inverse of relative wages. Demand for their products differs only because marginal costs differ, so relative productivity follows from income and wages:

A(i)A(j)=(L(i)w(i)σL(j)w(j)σ)1σ−1(47)\frac{A(i)}{A(j)}=\left(\frac{L(i)w(i)^{\sigma}}{L(j)w(j)^{\sigma}}\right)^{\frac{1}{\sigma-1}} \tag{47}A(j)A(i)​=(L(j)w(j)σL(i)w(i)σ​)σ−11​(47)

The model extends this logic to locations with different trade costs. In the estimates, composite amenities are much lower and composite productivities much higher in more populated counties. With α=0.1\alpha=0.1α=0.1 and β=−0.3\beta=-0.3β=−0.3, exogenous amenities are high in southern Florida, southern California and Arizona and low in the centre of the country; exogenous productivities are highest along the Eastern Seaboard and in the upper Midwest and low in Montana, Nebraska and west Texas; the correlation between the two is 0.12. The value of α\alphaα is somewhat above the 3 to 8 percent productivity gain from doubling population surveyed by Rosenthal and Strange (2004), to allow for entry effects that the perfectly competitive model omits. The value of β\betaβ comes from the housing isomorphism and a housing expenditure share of 18.7 to 24.7 percent, which implies a magnitude of 0.23 to 0.325.

With commuting costs set to ten times the estimated trade costs in ad valorem terms, estimated productivities are very similar to the baseline and estimated amenities are substantially smoother across space, because workers can earn the high wages of nearby locations.

Importance of Geographic Location

Adding the log-linear equations for wages and population gives an equation for income Y(i)≡w(i)L(i)Y(i)\equiv w(i)L(i)Y(i)≡w(i)L(i):

γ1σ−1ln⁡Y(i)=Cw+CLσ−1+(1−β)ln⁡Aˉ(i)+(1+α)ln⁡uˉ(i)−(2+α−β)ln⁡P(i)(51)\frac{\gamma_1}{\sigma-1}\ln Y(i)=\frac{C_w+C_L}{\sigma-1}+(1-\beta)\ln\bar{A}(i)+(1+\alpha)\ln\bar{u}(i)-(2+\alpha-\beta)\ln P(i) \tag{51}σ−1γ1​​lnY(i)=σ−1Cw​+CL​​+(1−β)lnAˉ(i)+(1+α)lnuˉ(i)−(2+α−β)lnP(i)(51)

Income is log-linear in local characteristics and in the price index. A Shapley decomposition (Shorrocks 2013) assigns the variance of log income to the two groups of regressors: it computes the expected marginal contribution of each group to the R-squared. Because α\alphaα and β\betaβ are not identified but are needed to compute Aˉ\bar{A}Aˉ and uˉ\bar{u}uˉ, the decomposition is reported for all combinations of α∈[0,1]\alpha\in[0,1]α∈[0,1] and β∈[−1,0]\beta\in[-1,0]β∈[−1,0]. Geographic location accounts for at least 20 percent of the spatial variation in income in 2000, and for upward of 70 percent when α=0.23\alpha=0.23α=0.23 and β=−0.14\beta=-0.14β=−0.14. Two caveats work in opposite directions: if the trade cost function is misspecified the price index is measured with error, the model loads the unexplained part on productivity and amenity, and the share of geography is biased downward; on the other hand, transport networks may be built toward productive places, so the price index may partly reflect local characteristics.

Removing the Interstate Highway System

The counterfactual recomputes TTT with the estimated cost parameters after deleting the interstate highways from the road network, keeping other highways, arterial roads and the other modes. For given α\alphaα and β\betaβ the exogenous Aˉ\bar{A}Aˉ and uˉ\bar{u}uˉ are held at their estimated values, and the new population, wages and welfare are computed from the Hammerstein equation and the change-of-variables relation. The exercise is repeated for combinations with α+β≤0\alpha+\beta\leq0α+β≤0, so that Theorem 2 guarantees uniqueness.

  • Price index: holding wages, population and productivities fixed, the price index rises most in the Rocky Mountains and least in California and on the Eastern Seaboard, which have better alternative modes and buy more from nearby producers.

  • Population: population moves toward California and the Eastern Seaboard and away from the Rocky Mountains. The reallocation has much more local variation with α=0.1\alpha=0.1α=0.1 and β=−0.3\beta=-0.3β=−0.3 than without spillovers.

  • Welfare: removing the system lowers welfare by 1.1 to 1.4 percent, depending on the strength of spillovers. This counts only the cost of trading goods, not passenger travel.

  • Cost-benefit comparison: construction cost 560 billion dollars (2007 dollars), or about 28 billion a year at a 5 percent cost of capital; maintenance of the whole highway system costs about 130 billion a year, of which half is attributed to the interstates; the total annual cost is therefore about 100 billion dollars. With GDP of 14.25 trillion dollars in 2007 and homothetic preferences, a welfare loss of 1.1 to 1.4 percent is worth 150 to 200 billion dollars a year. The benefits exceed the annual costs by at least 50 percent, an annualized return of at least 9 percent, computed as the net annual gain of 50 billion over the 560 billion of construction cost.

This is the primitive that defines preferences. A worker living in iii consumes a quantity q(s,i)q(s,i)q(s,i) of the variety produced in each location sss (per capita, so it is a density over sss), aggregates these with a constant elasticity of substitution σ>1\sigma>1σ>1, and the resulting consumption index is multiplied by the local amenity u(i)u(i)u(i). Welfare is therefore measured in units of the consumption aggregate scaled by amenity; only ratios of WWW across locations matter for location choice.

The CES form does three things. First, because every location makes its own variety (the Armington assumption) and σ<∞\sigma<\inftyσ<∞, consumers want a positive amount of every variety, so every location sells everywhere and bilateral trade flows take the gravity form of equation (3) with trade elasticity σ−1\sigma-1σ−1. Second, CES is homothetic, so maximized utility is income divided by a price index, which gives the indirect utility W(i)=w(i)u(i)/P(i)W(i)=w(i)u(i)/P(i)W(i)=w(i)u(i)/P(i) of equation (5). Third, the love of variety is what makes a location's product face a downward-sloping demand, which is the built-in dispersion force (the term 111 in γ1\gamma_1γ1​ of equation (15)).

Amenity enters multiplicatively, so it shifts the level of welfare without changing the composition of demand. As σ→∞\sigma\rightarrow\inftyσ→∞ varieties become perfect substitutes; as σ→1\sigma\rightarrow1σ→1 the aggregator becomes Cobb-Douglas. The planner's problem in equation (21) uses the same aggregator with qqq reinterpreted as total quantities.

These are assumed functional forms for how local population affects productivity and amenity. Aˉ(i)\bar{A}(i)Aˉ(i) and uˉ(i)\bar{u}(i)uˉ(i) are exogenous fundamentals of location iii; L(i)L(i)L(i) is the density of workers; α\alphaα is the elasticity of composite productivity A(i)A(i)A(i) with respect to local population and β\betaβ the elasticity of composite amenity u(i)u(i)u(i):

∂ln⁡A(i)∂ln⁡L(i)=α,∂ln⁡u(i)∂ln⁡L(i)=β\frac{\partial\ln A(i)}{\partial\ln L(i)}=\alpha,\qquad\frac{\partial\ln u(i)}{\partial\ln L(i)}=\beta∂lnL(i)∂lnA(i)​=α,∂lnL(i)∂lnu(i)​=β

The empirically relevant case is α≥0\alpha\geq0α≥0 (agglomeration economies) and β≤0\beta\leq0β≤0 (congestion). The spillovers are local: only the population of iii itself matters, not that of neighbours. They are external to the individual worker, who takes A(i)A(i)A(i) and u(i)u(i)u(i) as given, which is why the equilibrium is generally inefficient (equation (23)).

The isoelastic form is what keeps the model tractable: after substitution, the equilibrium conditions (11) and (12) remain power functions of LLL and www, and collapse to the Hammerstein equation (14), whose exponents depend on α\alphaα and β\betaβ only through γ1\gamma_1γ1​ and γ2\gamma_2γ2​ of equation (15). Setting α=β=0\alpha=\beta=0α=β=0 gives the linear model of equation (10).

This defines the geographic distance between two locations as the cost of the cheapest route. A path is a function g:[0,1]→Sg:[0,1]\rightarrow Sg:[0,1]→S with g(0)=ig(0)=ig(0)=i and g(1)=jg(1)=jg(1)=j; the variable ttt inside the integral is only the parameter of the path (not to be confused with the function t(i,j)t(i,j)t(i,j) on the left). τ(g(t))\tau\left(g(t)\right)τ(g(t)) is the instantaneous trade cost at the point currently being crossed, and ∥dg(t)dt∥dt\left\|\frac{dg(t)}{dt}\right\|dt​dtdg(t)​​dt is the Euclidean length of the small step, so the integral is the line integral of τ\tauτ along the path: cost per unit of distance times distance, summed over the route. The infimum over the set Γ(i,j)\Gamma(i,j)Γ(i,j) of admissible paths picks the least-cost route.

The value does not depend on how the path is parametrized, and it is symmetric, t(i,j)=t(j,i)t(i,j)=t(j,i)t(i,j)=t(j,i), because the reversed path has the same cost. It satisfies t(i,i)=0t(i,i)=0t(i,i)=0 and the triangle inequality t(i,k)≤t(i,j)+t(j,k)t(i,k)\leq t(i,j)+t(j,k)t(i,k)≤t(i,j)+t(j,k), since joining two routes is an admissible route. If τ\tauτ is a constant, the least-cost route is the straight line and

t(i,j)=τ∥i−j∥t(i,j)=\tau\left\|i-j\right\|t(i,j)=τ∥i−j∥

which is the case used on the line (equation (28)) and the circle. In general the route bends toward regions of low τ\tauτ such as roads. The function is the solution of the eikonal equation (25), which is what the Fast Marching Method computes, and it is mapped into an iceberg cost by T(i,j)=f(t(i,j))T(i,j)=f\left(t(i,j)\right)T(i,j)=f(t(i,j)), with the exponential form of equation (26). The gain is dimensionality: the function τ\tauτ on SSS determines the function TTT on S×SS\times SS×S.

Fix the origin iii and regard t(i,j)t(i,j)t(i,j) of equation (24) as a function of the destination jjj. The argument is dynamic programming. Take any small displacement hhh from jjj. One admissible route to j+hj+hj+h is the least-cost route to jjj followed by the straight segment from jjj to j+hj+hj+h, whose cost is τ(j)∥h∥\tau(j)\left\|h\right\|τ(j)∥h∥ to first order because τ\tauτ is continuous. Hence

t(i,j+h)≤t(i,j)+τ(j)∥h∥+o(∥h∥)t(i,j+h)\leq t(i,j)+\tau(j)\left\|h\right\|+o\left(\left\|h\right\|\right)t(i,j+h)≤t(i,j)+τ(j)∥h∥+o(∥h∥)

Where ttt is differentiable in jjj, t(i,j+h)=t(i,j)+∇t(i,j)⋅h+o(∥h∥)t(i,j+h)=t(i,j)+\nabla t(i,j)\cdot h+o\left(\left\|h\right\|\right)t(i,j+h)=t(i,j)+∇t(i,j)⋅h+o(∥h∥), so for every direction hhh

∇t(i,j)⋅h≤τ(j)∥h∥\nabla t(i,j)\cdot h\leq\tau(j)\left\|h\right\|∇t(i,j)⋅h≤τ(j)∥h∥

Choosing hhh parallel to the gradient gives ∥∇t(i,j)∥≤τ(j)\left\|\nabla t(i,j)\right\|\leq\tau(j)∥∇t(i,j)∥≤τ(j). For the reverse inequality, let jjj lie on the least-cost route to a slightly farther point and step backward along that route by hhh: by the principle of optimality the route up to j−hj-hj−h is itself optimal, so t(i,j)=t(i,j−h)+τ(j)∥h∥+o(∥h∥)t(i,j)=t(i,j-h)+\tau(j)\left\|h\right\|+o\left(\left\|h\right\|\right)t(i,j)=t(i,j−h)+τ(j)∥h∥+o(∥h∥), that is ∇t(i,j)⋅h=τ(j)∥h∥\nabla t(i,j)\cdot h=\tau(j)\left\|h\right\|∇t(i,j)⋅h=τ(j)∥h∥ for this direction, which by the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality requires ∥∇t(i,j)∥≥τ(j)\left\|\nabla t(i,j)\right\|\geq\tau(j)∥∇t(i,j)∥≥τ(j). Together:

∥∇t(i,j)∥=τ(j)\left\|\nabla t(i,j)\right\|=\tau(j)∥∇t(i,j)∥=τ(j)

with boundary condition t(i,i)=0t(i,i)=0t(i,i)=0. The gradient points along the optimal route and is orthogonal to the iso-cost contour {j∣t(i,j)=C}\left\{j|t(i,j)=C\right\}{j∣t(i,j)=C}. Moving a distance δ\deltaδ in that direction raises the cost by τ(j)δ\tau(j)\deltaτ(j)δ, so raising the contour level by ε\varepsilonε moves the contour outward by ε/τ(j)\varepsilon/\tau(j)ε/τ(j): the front advances at speed 1/τ(j)1/\tau(j)1/τ(j), which is exactly the step of the Fast Marching Method. At points where several optimal routes meet, ttt is not differentiable and the equation holds in the viscosity sense.

The exponential form is the continuous limit of compounding iceberg costs. ∏k=1n(1+τ(gk)Δk)=exp⁡(∑k=1nln⁡(1+τ(gk)Δk))\prod_{k=1}^{n}\left(1+\tau(g_k)\Delta_k\right)=\exp\left(\sum_{k=1}^{n}\ln\left(1+\tau(g_k)\Delta_k\right)\right)k=1∏n​(1+τ(gk​)Δk​)=exp(k=1∑n​ln(1+τ(gk​)Δk​))

Because the exponential is increasing, the path that minimizes the iceberg cost is the path that minimizes the integral, which by equation (24) equals t(i,j)t(i,j)t(i,j):
